tasks.judge_rationale: Response B ranks first because it addresses all four required vulnerabilities (parameterized queries, server-side object authorization, secrets management, and serializer allowlisting), whereas Response A is truncated mid-secret-configuration and never reaches the mass-assignment/serializer issue at all. Both are marred by errors (A mislinks CWE-89 to CWE-79 and CWE-862 to CWE-732; B imports a nonexistent `get_password_hash` and over-complicates the permission model with ambiguous `is_owner`/staff logic), and both are cut off at the end, but B's fuller coverage of the mandated scope makes it the more complete response.

Response A produced no answer (timeout), so it fails every criterion. Response B delivers a correct, well-reasoned atomic sliding-window limiter in Lua with explicit fail-open/fail-closed handling and a solid Lua-vs-pipeline discussion, but it is truncated before fully implementing the cache (single-flight, TTL jitter, stale-while-revalidate), per-class eviction policy, and failover counter-consistency analysis, which lowers its completeness.

Both apply the systematic method with likelihood-ranked hypotheses, but A delivers complete, idiomatic, and mostly-correct reproductions and fixes for all three tests. B contains concrete code bugs — its timezone reproduction can't actually fail (strftime on an already-UTC-aware datetime ignores system TZ) and its wait_for_condition helper returns a Task rather than the awaited result — and its explicit fixes section is truncated before it prescribes the fixes.
